frames.narration: A client wants to store a 720 MB video as photos/2026/10/a.mov. It starts a multipart upload, and the front end asks the metadata service for an upload id. Nothing is visible yet.
The client sends six parts of 120 MB in parallel. Each part is cut into 6 data pieces of 20 MB, and the coder computes 3 parity pieces of 20 MB.

The placement logic puts the 9 pieces of each part on 9 different racks, with a checksum for each piece. Six parts of 9 pieces make 54 pieces and 1,080 MB in total, which is 1.5 times the 720 MB of the object.

messages.label: 9 pieces of 20 MB, one per rack

frames.narration: The client calls complete with the six part numbers and checksums. The metadata service commits one record with all 54 piece locations. From this moment a get or a list will see the object.
Later, a disk in rack C dies. Heartbeats stop and the data node is declared failed. The metadata shows that this one disk held a piece of this object and of millions of others.

messages.label: disk 7 in rack C is gone

frames.narration: Eight pieces are enough, because only 6 are needed. The repair worker reads 6 pieces, 120 MB, rebuilds the missing 20 MB piece and writes it to another disk in rack C. The metadata is updated, and the object has 9 pieces again. Rebuilding 20 MB took 6 times as much reading.
Another client lists the prefix photos/2026/10/ with the delimiter '/'. The front end asks the sorted index for a range scan, which returns keys in order, 1,000 at most.
The page holds a.mov and its neighbours, plus a continuation token naming the last key returned. The next call starts after that key, so pages are stable even if new objects arrive.
